1	# Scraper
2	
3	Tools for scraping show data from [edfringe.com](https://www.edfringe.com).
4	
5	> For the API itself — endpoints, auth, the full `EventDetail` field surface, and
6	> the non-obvious bits (pricing lives behind a separate per-performance query;
7	> `ticketStatus` vs the `soldOut` flag) — see **[SCRAPING.md](SCRAPING.md)**.
8	
9	Three scripts, on three different clocks:
10	
11	| script | what it gets | how often |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| `fetch_shows.py` | the listing: shows, venues, genres | daily top-up, full rebuild on demand |
14	| `fetch_prices.py` | real ticket amounts, per show | **once** — prices don't move; see below |
15	| `normalize.py` | turns both into the committed site data | after either of the above |
16	
17	## How edfringe.com serves listings
18	
19	The "What's On" listing (`/tickets/whats-on?page=N`) is a **Next.js single-page
20	app**. The server returns the same ~20 KB JavaScript shell for every page and
21	the shows are loaded **client-side from a GraphQL API**. So fetching the HTML
22	yields empty pages — there is no show data in the markup to extract.
23	
24	The shows come from:
25	
26	```
27	POST https://edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com/graphql
28	```
29	
30	authenticated with a bearer token from `POST .../token` using the site's public
31	anonymous credentials. The `EventsSearch` operation returns structured JSON
32	(title, genre, dates, venues, spaces, performances, prices, images, …), 50
33	shows per page, ~3,800 shows over ~77 pages.
34	
35	## fetch_shows.py — download all shows from the API
36	
37	```
38	python3 scraper/fetch_shows.py
39	```
40	
41	- Authenticates, then pages through every show via the GraphQL API.
42	- Output (default `data/raw_pages/`):
43	  - `page_NN.json` — the raw `events` payload per page (kept for re-processing).
44	  - `shows.json` — all show results flattened into a single array.
45	- A random 4–9 s delay is inserted between requests.
46	- **Resumable**: existing `page_NN.json` files are skipped; use `--force` to
47	  re-fetch. A fixed `--seed` keeps the server ordering stable across pages so
48	  paging never skips or duplicates shows.
49	
50	Options:
51	
52	```
53	python3 scraper/fetch_shows.py \
54	    --per 50 --seed 123 --min-delay 4 --max-delay 9 \
55	    --out-dir data/raw_pages [--max-pages N] [--force]
56	```
57	
58	The raw output is **git-ignored** (see `.gitignore`) — it is a regenerable
59	cache, not source.
60	
61	## fetch_prices.py — real ticket prices, fetched once
62	
63	```bash
64	python3 scraper/fetch_prices.py --slug daniel-sloss-bitter   # one show
65	python3 scraper/fetch_prices.py --all                        # every paid show
66	python3 scraper/fetch_prices.py --selftest                   # offline transform test
67	```
68	
69	The listing API carries **no amounts** — `priceType` is a set of flags, which is
70	why the site knew only "free vs paid" for so long. Money comes from a separate
71	`performancePrices(performanceRef)` query, **one call per performance**, with no
72	bulk endpoint. Price *bands* are set per show and repeat across its
73	performances, so one call per show is enough; `--sample-performances N` prices N
74	of a show's performances and reports whether the bands actually agree.
75	
76	Output is `data/prices.json` — **committed, and fetched once**:
77	
78	```json
79	{"v": 1, "fetchedAt": "2026-07-30",
80	 "shows": {"2026DANIELS": {"min": 22.5, "max": 29.5, "fee": 1.5,
81	                           "bands": [{"type": "Price C", "value": 22.5}, …],
82	                           "slug": "daniel-sloss-bitter", "ref": "1:790001"}}}
83	```
84	
85	Why once, and why it is *not* on the nightly path:
86	
87	- **A show's price doesn't move.** Ticket *status* changes hourly (hence
88	  `refresh-tickets`) and the listing gains shows daily (hence `refresh-shows`),
89	  but the bands a show sells at are set when it goes on sale. Re-fetching them
90	  nightly would be ~3,500 API calls a day to re-learn the same numbers.
91	- **The pass is resumable.** Shows already in the cache are skipped, so `--limit
92	  N` takes the festival in bites and `--force` re-prices deliberately. The cache
93	  is rewritten every 25 shows, so a mid-run crash loses at most that many —
94	  but note what "resumable" is measured against: **the cache file on disk**. On
95	  a runner that file is only durable once the workflow's commit step pushes it,
96	  which it does at the end of the job (including when the fetch step failed).
97	  Against a *script* failure that is enough; against the runner itself dying,
98	  nothing in the job runs and the whole run is lost. If that matters, chunk the
99	  festival with `limit` — each run commits what it got.
100	- **Free shows are skipped**, not called: there is nothing to price, and
101	  `normalize.py` already reads £0 off the listing's `free` flag.
102	- **A missing show means the price is unknown, not free.** The festival keeps
103	  adding shows after the price run, so gaps are normal and permanent. Every
104	  consumer treats unknown as its own state (`shared/price.js`).
105	
106	Run it on a runner via the **`Fetch ticket prices (one-off)`** workflow
107	(`.github/workflows/prices.yml`), which fetches, regenerates and commits.
108	
109	## normalize.py — turn the raw scrape into website data
110	
111	```
112	python3 scraper/normalize.py
113	```
114	
115	Reads the raw scrape and emits the site's data layers (these **are** committed,
116	since the site serves them):
117	
118	| file | purpose | sent to browser |
119	|---|---|---|
120	| `data/normalized/shows.json` | master: one record per show with all performances (including each show's full `description`); source for regenerating everything below | no |
121	| `data/normalized/shows.min.json` | the compact catalogue the planner downloads (3.0 MB, 948 KB gzipped): the master packed losslessly against the `venues.json` lookups. Carries **no ticket status** — see the sidecar below — so an unchanged festival regenerates it byte-for-byte and the browser can hold it for 4 days | yes (planner) |
122	| `data/normalized/availability.min.json` | `{v, ts, a: {show id → {"MMDD\|HH:MM" → status index}}, o}` — per-performance ticket status, split out of the catalogue because it is the one thing that moves hourly. Self-contained (its own status list, indexes into nothing), 149 KB gzipped, cached for 1 day | yes (planner) |
123	| `data/normalized/descriptions.min.json` | `{v, d: {slug → full description}}`, kept out of the catalogue above so that file stays small enough to block on. Fetched lazily by the planner and cached for a week; the hover card and search fall back to the catalogue's 160-char `blurb` until it lands | yes (planner, lazily) |
124	| `data/venues.json` | shared lookup sent once: `{ venues, rooms, genres, subgenres, ticketStatuses }` — venue map (code → name, address, postcode, lat, lng) plus the global lookup lists | yes (once) |
125	| `data/days/2026-08-DD.json` | per-day shows with the minimum a card needs (venue, genre, room, subgenres and ticket status referenced by index) | yes (today's) |
126	| `data/days/index.json` | available days + per-day counts | yes |
127	
128	`normalize.py` has a **second input** besides the raw scrape: `data/prices.json`
129	(above), which it folds into the master and both wire forms. It is an input, not
130	an output — `normalize.py` never writes it, and runs happily without it (every
131	show simply has an unknown price, and it says so).
132	
133	Normalization rules:
134	- **Location** = venue code (the "venue number") + the show's room (space); venue
135	  name/address/coords live only in `venues.json`.
136	- **Shared lookups live once, in `venues.json`.** It is a
137	  `{ "venues": {...}, "rooms": [...], "genres": [...] }` container: `rooms` and
138	  `genres` are the global de-duplicated string lists (~420 rooms, 10 genres).
139	  The browser already fetches this file once, so the lists cost one small
140	  download rather than being repeated in every day file.
141	- **Day files are compact.** Each `2026-08-DD.json` is a plain array of shows; a
142	  show's `genre`, `room`, `subs` (subgenres) and `ts` (ticket status) are indices

input.title: Cache each data file for as long as its contents last (fixes #249)
input.body:
GitHub Pages sets its own `Cache-Control` with no way to vary it per file, so the freshness policy now lives on the client in a new `shared/data-cache.js` (lifted out of `plan.js`, which already had most of it). Both pages use it, with a TTL per file instead of one blanket one.

| file | kept for | why |
|---|---|---|
| `shows.min.json` | **4 days** | 948 KB gzipped, and nothing in it changes through the day |
| `availability.min.json` | **1 day** | ticket status moves hourly; 149 KB gzipped |
| `venues.json` | 1 day | small, and the cached catalogue indexes into it |
| `days/2026-08-DD.json` | 1 day | carries ticket status; keyed by date, so this is within-the-day reuse |
| `descriptions.min.json` | 7 days | unchanged |

## The catalogue had to give something up first

`shows.min.json` couldn't earn a 4-day TTL while it carried per-performance ticket status — the one field that moves hourly. That's the same seam #249 is about, so the two are fixed together rather than against each other.

Ticket status moves out into `data/normalized/availability.min.json`: `{v, ts, a: {show id → {"MMDD|HH:MM" → status index}}, o}`. It's self-contained (its own status list, indexing into nothing) so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone, and the catalogue is now regenerated byte-for-byte identically over an unchanged festival — which is what makes holding it for days safe rather than merely cheap.

Performances are named by date + start rather than by array position, because the catalogue and the sidecar are cached on different clocks and get joined across generations. A show that gained or lost a date since the cached catalogue was written finds no status for the performances that moved, instead of silently inheriting its neighbour's. Four shows list the same date and start twice with genuinely different statuses; those get a `#n` suffix.

## Fixes #249

Both gaps in the issue, at the root:

- **The hourly refresh wrote a file the planner doesn't read.** `refresh_ticket_status.py` wrote only `data/days/*.json`; the planner has never loaded those. It now writes statuses through the master and regenerates every derived file from it, so one source of truth feeds all of them — and `worker.sh` stages `data/normalized` so the result actually ships.
- **Nothing refreshed future dates.** It stopped at today, leaving every later date frozen at the last manual full scrape. It now covers today through the end of the run. One listing pass already returned those performances, so the wider window costs nothing extra; the hourly frequency and the August/08:00–23:59 precondition are unchanged.

`refresh-shows` is left alone deliberately — `--recently-added LAST_SEVEN_DAYS` is a catalogue top-up and was never a source of fresh status. Widening it would duplicate `refresh-tickets` at a much higher fetch cost. Noted in its worker so the next reader doesn't re-lit ate it.

## Two invariants now hold this up

Both fail silently, so both are tested:

1. **`shows.min.json` carries nothing day-varying.** A status leaking back in would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for anyone holding a cached copy — #249 re-created from the other end. `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.
2. **The `venues.json` lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). A four-day-old catalogue is routinely decoded against a `venues.json` fetched today, so an entry that changed index would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never dropped, even once the master stops using them.

`edfringe-lookup-indices` was still probing `p[].t` on the catalogue; it now checks the sidecar's indices against that file's own `ts` list, and the live gate reads the real sidecar off disk.

## A pre-existing test failure, fixed

`shows.min.json rehydrates byte-identical to the master` was already red on `main` (177/178). It expected the master's `description` back out of the catalogue, which deliberately leaves that field to `descriptions.min.json`. It now strips the field and asserts it survives in that sidecar, so "moved" can't quietly become "lost". This is the guard the whole split relies on, so it needed to be green.

## Worth knowing

- Regenerating the day files from the master reverted two hourly ticket updates on `2026-08-04` and `2026-08-05` — both past dates. They existed only because the old refresh wrote day files without writing the master, which is the drift this PR removes.
- The committed `availability.min.json` is generated from the master, so its statuses are as stale as the last full scrape. The first `refresh-tickets` run on this branch's code is what makes them current; I can't reach the edfringe API from this session to do it here.
- A 1-day TTL on the now page's day file means a returning visitor within the same day won't see hourly status updates until the next day. That is what was asked for, and it's a real trade against the hourly job's purpose on that page. If you'd rather the now page stay live, the cheap change is a short TTL there (an hour) — the caching win on that page is mostly first-paint anyway, since it's a per-date URL.

## Testing

`npm run verify` — 194 tests, all passing (up from 178 with one failure). New: 8 tests for the cache layer (TTL suppression, expiry, per-url clocks, stale fallback, no-Cache-Storage degradation, failed writes), mutation-checked by breaking the TTL check and the stale fallback and confirming they go red. Plus sidecar join tests in `hydrate.test.mjs`, availability/append-only assertions in `normalize.py --selftest`, and updated pack checks.

---

content.content:
# Claudinite per-repo task scheduler — the repo's ONLY cron
# (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3). A thin shim: all logic lives in the
# vendored engine, so this file changes rarely (schema and behavior changes ride
# the vendor refresh, not edits here). It runs hourly on a repo-hashed minute
# constrained to :10–:50 — spreading the fleet, dodging GitHub's :00 stampede,
# and staying clear of the hour boundary the slot math anchors on.
#
# The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap/vendoring rewrites it to this
# repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by
# `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`
# (scheduler-workflow-shape enforces the range; baselining re-derives the value to
# catch drift). `workflow_dispatch` allows a manual run; the concurrency group
# serializes runs so a slow run and its successor never overlap.
#
# A manual run may carry `overrides` — ONE free-form `KEY=value` string, because
# GitHub cannot declare arbitrary named inputs. It reaches the engine as
# `CLAUDINITE_OVERRIDES`, and the engine understands exactly one key:
# `FORCE_TASKS=<comma-separated task ids>`.
# It runs those tasks even though their slot has already passed, and
# WITHOUT consulting their preconditions — forcing is the operator's decision, so
# nothing asks the task whether it agrees. The engine learns "run these ids",
# never what any of them do, and no task declaration mentions forcing at all.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '49 * * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      overrides:
        description: 'Manual-run overrides: comma-separated KEY=value. FORCE_TASKS=<task ids> runs those tasks unconditionally, even when their slot has passed, e.g. FORCE_TASKS=baselining.'
        required: false
        default: ''

concurrency:
  group: claudinite-scheduler
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write        # read the repo + vendored engine; baselining's deliver() pushes the maintenance branch (agent-preprocessing §7/E4)
  issues: write          # file / label / close dispatch issues
  pull-requests: write   # baselining's deliver() opens the per-cycle maintenance PR and arms auto-merge
  actions: write         # read the run ledger (last successful run) for due-slot math, AND
                         # dispatch a workflow a task drives (store-release fires the release
                         # orchestrator's daily leg) — creating a workflow_dispatch event needs
                         # write, not read, and `read` silently 403s the POST

jobs:
  schedule:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Evaluate schedule and dispatch due tasks
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # Empty on every scheduled run — `inputs` is only populated by
          # workflow_dispatch. The engine reads only FORCE_TASKS out of it.
          CLAUDINITE_OVERRIDES: ${{ inputs.overrides }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/run.mjs

  # A scheduled run reaches no one when it goes red, so escalate a whole-run
  # failure to a human-visible `workflow-failure` issue (DESIGN §3.6,
  # gha/scheduled-failure-escalation). Converges to ONE open issue by a fixed
  # title (create-or-comment), and ensures the label first since a first-run
  # failure may precede the scheduler's own label-ensure.
  report-failure:
    needs: schedule
    if: failure()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite scheduler run failed';
            await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' }).catch(() => {});
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${owner}/${repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            const body = `The Claudinite scheduler run failed: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels: ['workflow-failure'], body });

content.text: The refresh worked and the numbers confirm the fix. Updating the PR body — two of its statements are now out of date.

input.body:
GitHub Pages sets its own `Cache-Control` with no way to vary it per file, so the freshness policy now lives on the client in a new `shared/data-cache.js` (lifted out of `plan.js`, which already had most of it). Both pages use it, with a TTL per file instead of one blanket one.

| file | kept for | why |
|---|---|---|
| `shows.min.json` | **4 days** | 948 KB gzipped, and nothing in it changes through the day |
| `availability.min.json` | **1 day** | ticket status moves hourly; 149 KB gzipped |
| `venues.json` | 1 day | small, and the cached catalogue indexes into it |
| `days/2026-08-DD.json` | **1 hour** | the now page's premise is live availability, and `refresh-tickets` rewrites this hourly — the TTL tracks the refresh that feeds it |
| `descriptions.min.json` | 7 days | unchanged |

## The catalogue had to give something up first

`shows.min.json` couldn't earn a 4-day TTL while it carried per-performance ticket status — the one field that moves hourly. That's the same seam #249 is about, so the two are fixed together rather than against each other.

Ticket status moves out into `data/normalized/availability.min.json`: `{v, ts, a: {show id → {"MMDD|HH:MM" → status index}}, o}`. It's self-contained (its own status list, indexing into nothing) so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone, and the catalogue is now regenerated byte-for-byte identically over an unchanged festival — which is what makes holding it for days safe rather than merely cheap.

Performances are named by date + start rather than by array position, because the catalogue and the sidecar are cached on different clocks and get joined across generations. A show that gained or lost a date since the cached catalogue was written finds no status for the performances that moved, instead of silently inheriting its neighbour's. Four shows list the same date and start twice with genuinely different statuses; those get a `#n` suffix.

## Fixes #249

Both gaps in the issue, at the root:

- **The hourly refresh wrote a file the planner doesn't read.** `refresh_ticket_status.py` wrote only `data/days/*.json`; the planner has never loaded those. It now writes statuses through the master and regenerates every derived file from it, so one source of truth feeds all of them — and `worker.sh` stages `data/normalized` so the result actually ships.
- **Nothing refreshed future dates.** It stopped at today, leaving every later date frozen at the last manual full scrape. It now covers today through the end of the run. One listing pass already returned those performances, so the wider window costs nothing extra; the hourly frequency and the August/08:00–23:59 precondition are unchanged.

`refresh-shows` is left alone deliberately — `--recently-added LAST_SEVEN_DAYS` is a catalogue top-up and was never a source of fresh status. Widening it would duplicate `refresh-tickets` at a much higher fetch cost. Noted in its worker so the next reader doesn't re-litigate it.

### Verified against the live API

`refresh-tickets` was force-dispatched on this branch ([run 31182350551](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/actions/runs/31182350551), commit `d9ec105`). It behaved exactly as designed:

- **1,056 performance statuses moved**, spread across all 25 remaining dates — not just today. Mostly `TICKETS_AVAILABLE → NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` (731) and `TWO_FOR_ONE → NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` (231), i.e. exactly the stale-showing-as-bookable direction the issue reported.
- `amanda-knox-cartwheel`, the issue's worked example, now reads `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` across its whole run instead of going blue from 08-09 onward.
- **`shows.min.json` came back byte-identical** and is absent from the commit, which is the property the 4-day TTL rests on. The commit touches only the master, the sidecar, and the 25 day files from today forward; past dates, `venues.json` and `descriptions.min.json` are untouched.

## Two invariants now hold this up

Both fail silently, so both are tested:

1. **`shows.min.json` carries nothing day-varying.** A status leaking back in would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for anyone holding a cached copy — #249 re-created from the other end. `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.
2. **The `venues.json` lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). A four-day-old catalogue is routinely decoded against a `venues.json` fetched today, so an entry that changed index would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never dropped, even once the master stops using them.

`edfringe-lookup-indices` was still probing `p[].t` on the catalogue; it now checks the sidecar's indices against that file's own `ts` list, and the live gate reads the real sidecar off disk.

## A pre-existing test failure, fixed

`shows.min.json rehydrates byte-identical to the master` was already red on `main` (177/178). It expected the master's `description` back out of the catalogue, which deliberately leaves that field to `descriptions.min.json`. It now strips the field and asserts it survives in that sidecar, so "moved" can't quietly become "lost". This is the guard the whole split relies on, so it needed to be green.

## Worth knowing

Regenerating the day files from the master reverted two hourly ticket updates on `2026-08-04` and `2026-08-05` — both past dates. They existed only because the old refresh wrote day files without writing the master, which is precisely the drift this PR removes.

## Testing

`npm run verify` — 194 tests, all passing (up from 178 with one failure), re-run against the refreshed data. New: 8 tests for the cache layer (TTL suppression, expiry, per-url clocks, stale fallback, no-Cache-Storage degradation, failed writes), mutation-checked by breaking the TTL check and the stale fallback and confirming they go red. Plus sidecar join tests in `hydrate.test.mjs`, availability/append-only assertions in `normalize.py --selftest`, and updated pack checks.

content.text: Comment class: process-change — an owner-triggered merge command.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/EdFringeNow/.claude/skills/merge-to-main

The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

input.body:
GitHub Pages sets its own `Cache-Control` with no way to vary it per file, so the freshness policy now lives on the client in a new `shared/data-cache.js` (lifted out of `plan.js`, which already had most of it). Both pages use it, with a TTL per file instead of one blanket one.

| file | kept for | why |
|---|---|---|
| `shows.min.json` | **4 days** | 948 KB gzipped, and nothing in it changes through the day |
| `availability.min.json` | **1 day** | ticket status moves hourly; 149 KB gzipped |
| `venues.json` | 1 day | small, and the cached catalogue indexes into it |
| `days/2026-08-DD.json` | **1 hour** | the now page's premise is live availability, and `refresh-tickets` rewrites this hourly — the TTL tracks the refresh that feeds it |
| `descriptions.min.json` | 7 days | unchanged |

## The catalogue had to give something up first

`shows.min.json` couldn't earn a 4-day TTL while it carried per-performance ticket status — the one field that moves hourly. That's the same seam #249 is about, so the two are fixed together rather than against each other.

Ticket status moves out into `data/normalized/availability.min.json`: `{v, ts, a: {show id → {"MMDD|HH:MM" → status index}}, o}`. It's self-contained (its own status list, indexing into nothing) so the hourly refresh can rewrite it alone, and the catalogue is now regenerated byte-for-byte identically over an unchanged festival — which is what makes holding it for days safe rather than merely cheap.

Performances are named by date + start rather than by array position, because the catalogue and the sidecar are cached on different clocks and get joined across generations. A show that gained or lost a date since the cached catalogue was written finds no status for the performances that moved, instead of silently inheriting its neighbour's. Four shows list the same date and start twice with genuinely different statuses; those get a `#n` suffix.

## The refresh pipeline

Both gaps in the issue, at the root:

- **The hourly refresh wrote a file the planner doesn't read.** `refresh_ticket_status.py` wrote only `data/days/*.json`; the planner has never loaded those. It now writes statuses through the master and regenerates every derived file from it, so one source of truth feeds all of them — and `worker.sh` stages `data/normalized` so the result actually ships.
- **Nothing refreshed future dates.** It stopped at today, leaving every later date frozen at the last manual full scrape. It now covers today through the end of the run. One listing pass already returned those performances, so the wider window costs nothing extra; the hourly frequency and the August/08:00–23:59 precondition are unchanged.

`refresh-shows` is left alone deliberately — `--recently-added LAST_SEVEN_DAYS` is a catalogue top-up and was never a source of fresh status. Widening it would duplicate `refresh-tickets` at a much higher fetch cost. Noted in its worker so the next reader doesn't re-litigate it.

### Verified against the live API

`refresh-tickets` was force-dispatched on this branch ([run 31182350551](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/actions/runs/31182350551), commit `d9ec105`). It behaved exactly as designed:

- **1,056 performance statuses moved**, spread across all 25 remaining dates — not just today. Mostly `TICKETS_AVAILABLE → NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` (731) and `TWO_FOR_ONE → NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` (231), i.e. exactly the stale-showing-as-bookable direction the issue reported.
- `amanda-knox-cartwheel`, the issue's worked example, now reads `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` across its whole run instead of going blue from 08-09 onward.
- **`shows.min.json` came back byte-identical** and is absent from the commit, which is the property the 4-day TTL rests on. The commit touches only the master, the sidecar, and the 25 day files from today forward; past dates, `venues.json` and `descriptions.min.json` are untouched.

## Two invariants now hold this up

Both fail silently, so both are tested:

1. **`shows.min.json` carries nothing day-varying.** A status leaking back in would restart its hourly churn *and* freeze availability for anyone holding a cached copy — #249 re-created from the other end. `hydrate.test.mjs` asserts each wire performance carries only `d` and `s`.
2. **The `venues.json` lookup lists are append-only** (`extend_lookup`). A four-day-old catalogue is routinely decoded against a `venues.json` fetched today, so an entry that changed index would relabel shows' genres and rooms with no error anywhere. Entries are never dropped, even once the master stops using them.

`edfringe-lookup-indices` was still probing `p[].t` on the catalogue; it now checks the sidecar's indices against that file's own `ts` list, and the live gate reads the real sidecar off disk.

## A pre-existing test failure, fixed

`shows.min.json rehydrates byte-identical to the master` was already red on `main` (177/178). It expected the master's `description` back out of the catalogue, which deliberately leaves that field to `descriptions.min.json`. It now strips the field and asserts it survives in that sidecar, so "moved" can't quietly become "lost". This is the guard the whole split relies on, so it needed to be green.

## Worth knowing

Regenerating the day files from the master reverted two hourly ticket updates on `2026-08-04` and `2026-08-05` — both past dates. They existed only because the old refresh wrote day files without writing the master, which is precisely the drift this PR removes.

## Testing

`npm run verify` — 194 tests, all passing (up from 178 with one failure), re-run against the refreshed data. New: 8 tests for the cache layer (TTL suppression, expiry, per-url clocks, stale fallback, no-Cache-Storage degradation, failed writes), mutation-checked by breaking the TTL check and the stale fallback and confirming they go red. Plus sidecar join tests in `hydrate.test.mjs`, availability/append-only assertions in `normalize.py --selftest`, and updated pack checks.

Closes #249

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	#
3	# refresh-shows worker — the ported body of the retired
4	# "Refresh edfringe shows (daily)" workflow's job.
5	#
6	# The Claudinite scheduler runs this as its `prework` subprocess with
7	# cwd = this task directory and a hard kill at `prework_timeout`, so
8	# the first thing it does is move to the repo root the scheduler hands it. There
9	# is no agent: a non-zero exit is the failure signal, and the scheduler converges
10	# that to one open `needs-human` issue (the old job's `report-failure` twin).
11	#
12	# Lightweight top-up: fetch only shows added/updated in the last seven days,
13	# merge them into the existing normalized master, regenerate the venue + per-day
14	# files, and commit any changes.
15	#

30	// August, and the local hours the retired crons covered. The old lines fired at
31	// UTC hours 7…22 inclusive — sixteen firings — which is local 08:xx…23:xx.
32	export const FESTIVAL_MONTH = 8;
33	export const FIRST_LOCAL_HOUR = 8;
34	export const LAST_LOCAL_HOUR = 23;
35	
36	// Europe/London is UTC+1 for the ENTIRE window, so the conversion is a fixed
37	// one-hour shift and needs no timezone database. British Summer Time runs from
38	// the last Sunday in March to the last Sunday in October, so August lies strictly
39	// inside it with months of margin on both sides — there is no DST boundary
40	// anywhere near this window, and any instant whose Edinburgh wall clock reads
41	// August is necessarily under BST. (Instants that shift into any other month are
42	// rejected by the month test regardless, so the offset cannot matter there.)
43	// This is the correction the port had to get right: the scheduler's slot math is
44	// UTC, and reading the UTC hour as if it were local would shift the whole
45	// festival window an hour early.
46	const BST_OFFSET_MS = 60 * 60 * 1000;
47	
48	// The Edinburgh wall-clock month (1–12) and hour (0–23) at UTC instant `now`.
49	export function edinburghClock(now) {
50	  const local = new Date(new Date(now).getTime() + BST_OFFSET_MS);
51	  return { month: local.getUTCMonth() + 1, hour: local.getUTCHours() };
52	}
53	
54	// The precondition's verdict as a pure function of the instant — `{ run, reason }`.
55	export function ticketWindow(now) {
56	  const { month, hour } = edinburghClock(now);
57	  const clock = `${String(hour).padStart(2, '0')}:xx Edinburgh, month ${month}`;
58	  if (month !== FESTIVAL_MONTH) {
59	    return { run: false, reason: `outside the festival — ${clock}; ticket status only moves during August` };
60	  }
61	  // The upper bound is the last hour of the day, so it excludes nothing a
62	  // 0–23 hour could be; it is stated so the window's intent survives an edit.
63	  if (hour < FIRST_LOCAL_HOUR || hour > LAST_LOCAL_HOUR) {
64	    return { run: false, reason: `outside the daily window — ${clock}; the box office moves between ${FIRST_LOCAL_HOUR}:00 and ${LAST_LOCAL_HOUR}:59` };
65	  }
66	  return { run: true, reason: `in-festival and in-window — ${clock}` };
67	}

2	# (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3). A thin shim: all logic lives in the
3	# vendored engine, so this file changes rarely (schema and behavior changes ride
4	# the vendor refresh, not edits here). It runs hourly on a repo-hashed minute
5	# constrained to :10–:50 — spreading the fleet, dodging GitHub's :00 stampede,
6	# and staying clear of the hour boundary the slot math anchors on.

8	# The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap/vendoring rewrites it to this
9	# repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by

11	# (scheduler-workflow-shape enforces the range; baselining re-derives the value to
12	# catch drift). `workflow_dispatch` allows a manual run; the concurrency group
13	# serializes runs so a slow run and its successor never overlap.
14	#
15	# A manual run may carry `overrides` — ONE free-form `KEY=value` string, because
16	# GitHub cannot declare arbitrary named inputs. It reaches the engine as
17	# `CLAUDINITE_OVERRIDES`, and the engine understands exactly one key:
18	# `FORCE_TASKS=<comma-separated task ids>`.
19	# It runs those tasks even though their slot has already passed, and
20	# WITHOUT consulting their preconditions — forcing is the operator's decision, so
21	# nothing asks the task whether it agrees. The engine learns "run these ids",
22	# never what any of them do, and no task declaration mentions forcing at all.

29	    inputs:
30	      overrides:
31	        description: 'Manual-run overrides: comma-separated KEY=value. FORCE_TASKS=<task ids> runs those tasks unconditionally, even when their slot has passed, e.g. FORCE_TASKS=baselining.'
32	        required: false
33	        default: ''

37	  cancel-in-progress: false

41	  issues: write          # file / label / close dispatch issues
42	  pull-requests: write   # baselining's deliver() opens the per-cycle maintenance PR and arms auto-merge
43	  actions: write         # read the run ledger (last successful run) for due-slot math, AND
44	                         # dispatch a workflow a task drives (store-release fires the release
45	                         # orchestrator's daily leg) — creating a workflow_dispatch event needs
46	                         # write, not read, and `read` silently 403s the POST
